descripcion:
Before dessert, Cella says one thank-you out loud, then sends it. Say one thank-you out loud before dessert. Send this to whoever gets your thank-you.

The study: in three experiments, people wrote gratitude letters and then guessed how the receivers would feel. They underestimated how positive receivers would feel and overestimated how awkward it would be. The limit: the experiments were online and tested written letters, not a thank-you said out loud at a table. Cella's scene is a story, not a result.
Kumar, A., & Epley, N. (2018). Undervaluing gratitude: Expressers misunderstand the consequences of showing appreciation. Psychological Science, 29(9), 1423-1435. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797618772506

alt: A short film with a voice on a flat pink background in a dining room. At the top, the question: what do you do before dessert? A small ink-black doorway-shaped figure with white eyes stands beside a wooden table with a steaming pie and a phone. The words appear one line at a time: I say one thank-you out loud (the figure bobs and a speech bubble says: thank you). Then I send it (it taps the phone and a little envelope arcs off to the right). Patience, pie (the pie jiggles and the figure holds up a palm, then smiles). The closing question: who gets my thank-you? Then: Closer to yourself.
